lead: The Fifth Sunday of Easter turns from the appearances of the Risen Lord to the life of his body, the Church. Saul, the persecutor who has met the Lord, cannot get in through the door of the Jerusalem community until Barnabas takes him by the hand. John’s letter says that love is shown in deeds, and that whoever keeps the commandment abides in God. In the Gospel Jesus gives the image that holds it all together: the vine and the branches.

The word that runs through the letter and the Gospel is abide. The psalm is the last part of Psalm 22, the psalm whose opening cry Jesus prayed on the Cross. Here it ends in praise in the great assembly, with the ends of the earth turning to the Lord. The Church of Acts, growing in Judea, Galilee and Samaria, is the beginning of that answer.

set: Saul has met the Risen Lord on the road to Damascus (9:1–19), has preached in the synagogues there that Jesus is the Son of God (9:20), and has escaped a plot by being let down the city wall in a basket (9:23–25). Luke now brings him to Jerusalem. Paul’s own account in Galatians 1:17–19 adds that he first went away into Arabia, and that it was after three years that he went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas, staying fifteen days and seeing James the Lord’s brother. Luke tells it more briefly and keeps his eye on one thing: how the former persecutor was received.

Background. Barnabas first appears in 4:36–37: a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet. The apostles called him Barnabas, which Luke explains as “son of encouragement”. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem. Stephen had argued with members of their synagogues (6:9), and Saul had stood by at his death (7:58; 8:1). Now Saul takes Stephen’s place in the same debate and meets the same danger.
str: v. 26: Saul tries to join the disciples, and they are afraid of him.
v. 27: Barnabas brings him to the apostles and speaks for him.
vv. 28–29: Saul speaks boldly in Jerusalem and argues with the Hellenists, who try to kill him.
v. 30: the believers bring him down to Caesarea and send him to Tarsus.
v. 31: the Church has peace, is built up and grows.
¶ Verse 31 is one of Luke’s short summaries, like 2:42–47, 4:32–35 and 6:7. They are pauses in the story that show the whole Church at a glance.
kw: Used twice here (vv. 27, 28). The noun parrēsia means plain, fearless speech, the courage of the apostles before the council (4:13, 29, 31). The same noun is the “boldness before God” of today’s second reading (1 John 3:21).

The Church grows “in the comfort of the Holy Spirit” (v. 31). Luke explains the name Barnabas as “son of paraklēsis” (4:36). The word belongs to the same family as Paraclete, the name Jesus gives the Spirit in John. Barnabas does on earth what the Spirit does in the whole Church.

In the best manuscripts the word is singular: “the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria”. Later manuscripts have the plural, “churches”. The singular shows one Church spread over several regions.
vv: they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple.
Their fear was reasonable. He had dragged men and women off to prison (8:3). A conversion can be real and still need time before others can trust it.
But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles,

Barnabas risks his own good name. He listens to Saul’s story and then tells it for him: the road, the Lord who spoke, the bold preaching in Damascus. Every parish needs someone who will take the newcomer by the hand.
they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

Caesarea was the Roman port on the coast. Tarsus in Cilicia was Saul’s home city (21:39). He disappears from the story for some years, until Barnabas goes to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (11:25–26). Barnabas opens the door a second time.
Living in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.
Two things that seem opposed stand together: fear of the Lord, which is reverence, and comfort. The Church’s growth here comes from the Spirit, not from strategy.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of faith in Jesus as the Son of God, recalls Paul’s encounter on the road to Damascus and his first preaching that Jesus is the Son of God (CCC 442). The Church honours Barnabas, whom Acts calls an apostle (14:14), with a memorial on 11 June. In him she sees the ministry of welcome and encouragement: the one who believed in another’s conversion before the others did. Saul’s story also shows that the Church is not a club of the deserving. It is the place where an enemy can become a brother.

set: The First Letter of John comes from the tradition of the beloved disciple and was probably written near the end of the first century. Ancient tradition ascribes it to the apostle John; the letter does not name its writer, and many scholars think it comes from a disciple within the circle of John. It speaks to communities shaken after some members had left them (2:19). Its two great concerns are true faith in Jesus who has come in the flesh (4:2) and real love for brothers and sisters.

Just before our passage, John says that we know love because Christ laid down his life for us, and asks how God’s love can abide in anyone who sees a brother or sister in need and refuses help (3:16–17). Today’s verses follow from that.
str: v. 18: love in deeds, not only in words.
vv. 19–20: a troubled heart, and God who is greater than our hearts.
vv. 21–22: boldness before God and prayer that is heard.
v. 23: one commandment with two sides: believe in the name of the Son, and love one another.
v. 24: abiding in God, and the Spirit as the sign.
kw: For John, truth is not only correct words. It is what is real, and it comes from God. To love “in truth” is to love in a way that is real, and to be “from the truth” (v. 19) is to belong to God.
Confidence before God, the openness of a child who can speak to a father without fear (v. 21). The same word describes the apostles’ bold speech in Acts.

One of John’s favourite words, here in v. 24 and again and again in today’s Gospel passage. It means to stay, to dwell, to make one’s home. Christian life is not a visit to God but a remaining with him.
vv: Little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action.
“Little children” is the tender address of an old teacher. The verse does not despise words; it asks that they be true, and true words become deeds.
whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

The verse is a comfort. Our own heart can accuse us too much, or too little. God’s knowledge is larger than our self-condemnation, and his mercy is larger still. The Catechism quotes these words when it speaks of God’s holiness and mercy (CCC 208), and again when it speaks of conscience (CCC 1781).
And this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another,
The commandment is singular, yet it has two sides. Faith and love are not two separate tasks. Faith in the Son who loved us becomes love for one another.
And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit that he has given us.
The first mention of the Spirit in the letter. The sign that God dwells in us is not a feeling of our own making but a gift we have received.
ch: St Augustine preached ten homilies on this letter during Easter time. In one of them he gives the famous saying “Love, and do what you will”, meaning that if the root within is love, nothing but good can come from it (in substance). He did not mean that anything goes. He meant that love is the root from which every good act must grow, which is exactly the teaching of v. 18. The Church reads this letter in the Easter season because it shows what the new life of Easter looks like day by day: faith in the Son, love that acts, and the Spirit abiding within.

r.h: I am the vine, you are the branches
set: We are at the Last Supper, in the long farewell discourse of John 13–17. At the end of chapter 14 Jesus says, “Rise, let us be on our way” (14:31), and yet the discourse continues. Many scholars think chapters 15–17 were added to the first discourse as the Gospel took shape; others think the words were spoken on the way. Either way, the Church receives them as the Lord’s farewell teaching.

Background. In the Old Testament Israel is God’s vine, planted with love and tended with care, yet often disappointing: Isaiah 5:1–7, Psalm 80:8–16, Jeremiah 2:21. The Jewish historian Josephus describes a great golden vine over the entrance of the Temple sanctuary. When Jesus says “I am the true vine”, he presents himself as the faithful Israel in person, and his disciples belong to God’s people by belonging to him. This is the last of the seven “I am” sayings in John with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, and vine.
str: vv. 1–3: the vine, the vinegrower and the pruning; the disciples already cleansed by the word.
vv. 4–5: “Abide in me”: the branch lives only on the vine.
v. 6: the branch that does not abide.
vv. 7–8: prayer that is answered, much fruit, and the Father glorified.
kw: “True” in John means real, the genuine thing of which others were signs, as in “the true light” (1:9) and “the true bread from heaven” (6:32).

A play on words in the Greek. The Father “prunes” (kathairei, v. 2) the fruitful branch, and the disciples are already “cleansed” (katharoi, v. 3) by the word. Pruning and cleansing are the same action of love.
The key word of the passage, repeated again and again in vv. 4–7. It is not an effort to cling but a staying put: in his word, in his love, in his sacraments, in his Church.
vv: I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.
The Father is not far away. He is the one with his hands in the soil, looking after every branch.
Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
Any farmer in Kerala knows that a plant cut back grows stronger. Pruning hurts, but it is a sign that the vinegrower expects more fruit, not a sign of his anger.
I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
St Augustine notes that the Lord did not say “without me you can do little”, but “nothing” (in substance). The branch does not produce the sap; it receives it.
Whoever does not abide in me is thrown away like a branch and withers;

Vine wood is useless for building; Ezekiel says that no peg can be made of it (Ezekiel 15:2–5). Augustine says that the branch has only two places to be, either in the vine or in the fire (in substance).
My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.
The fruit is not success in the world’s sense. It is the life of a disciple. Even at the end of the Gospel, being a disciple is still something we “become”.
ch: The Second Vatican Council lists the vine among the images of the Church: Christ is the true vine who gives life and fruitfulness to the branches, that is, to us, who through the Church abide in him (Lumen Gentium 6). The Catechism quotes vv. 4–5 to describe the intimate communion between Christ and those who follow him (CCC 787), and it explains that the fruit spoken of here is the holiness of a life made fruitful by union with Christ (CCC 2074). The Church has always heard in the vine a hint of the Eucharist too: the cup of the fruit of the vine which becomes his blood is the sap that runs through the branches.

qa: Does “apart from me you can do nothing” mean that our efforts do not matter?

No. It means that even our good efforts are a gift. The Catechism teaches that God’s grace comes first and prepares us, and that God’s initiative calls for our own real response (CCC 2001–2002). The branch truly bears the fruit, but only because the sap of the vine is running in it.

It is a serious warning. To cut oneself off from Christ ends in loss, and the Church teaches that a person who dies refusing God’s love by mortal sin remains separated from him for ever (CCC 1033). But the verse names no one. It is spoken to disciples so that they may abide. While we live, the way back to the vine is always open through repentance and the sacrament of reconciliation.
Why were the disciples so slow to receive Saul?

Because they had suffered from him. Fear after real harm is not a sin. What Acts shows is the way through it: someone who knew both sides, Barnabas, took the risk of trust and spoke for him. Communities today face the same task when someone who once did harm comes back changed.
rite: In the Easter season the Paschal candle stands near the ambo or the altar until Pentecost, a sign that the Risen Lord is present among us. At the preparation of the gifts the priest blesses God for the wine, “fruit of the vine and work of human hands”, which will become our spiritual drink: the vine of today’s Gospel comes to the altar. In Year B every Sunday of Easter except the Third takes its Gospel from John, and on Wednesday this week the Mass will read the same passage of the vine again. At home, the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost.
study: Who is the Saul in my parish or family, the person others are slow to trust? Could I be a Barnabas for him or her?
John asks for love “in truth and action”. Which kind words of mine need to become a deed this week?
What pruning has God done in my life, and what fruit has come of it?
How do I abide in the vine: in prayer, in the Word, in the Eucharist, in the community? Which of these is weakest in me now?
